feed.subtitle: Building, operating, and learning in a home lab.

entry.title: AriseOne and the first repeatable jobs

link.title: AriseOne and the first repeatable jobs

entry.content:
AriseOne is the earliest chapter for which I have both working records and a later account of how the pieces fit together. The retrospective places the first workspace setup on January 16. The January 20 repository entries supply firmer markers: health and network checks, an Ansible inventory, and system update work. The archive folder itself dates to December, but a folder can exist before any of the work inside it. January is where the story has enough evidence to start.

The health checks and inventory served different purposes. A check could capture a condition at the time it ran. An inventory gave the same job a consistent list of systems to act on. Writing update work in Ansible made the intended action easier to repeat and inspect. The early records show that direction. They do not show that all updates were unattended or that every system was covered by the same checks.

In the February 3 to 5 account, Proxmox becomes the center of the lab. Homepage gives the services a front door, Nextcloud adds file service, and Zammad becomes the place to record support work. This is also where the limitations of the setup appear. NVIDIA drivers needed attention after kernel updates. The retrospective describes a repair script and a connection to ticket triggers. I can tell that the repair was written down and that a trigger was part of the design. I can’t reconstruct a complete unattended repair from the records I have.

By February 7 and 8, the documented routine was to look in the ticket system or knowledge base before making a change. A migration moved Markdown notes into Zammad’s knowledge base. The point was practical. A recurring problem needed a history that could be searched, and a repair needed enough context to be repeated. Keeping those notes alongside the services mattered more as one change began affecting several parts of the lab.

When it came time for a fresh start, AriseOne was still part of my history. Proxmox, monitoring, and ticketing appear again in the next set of records. Their reappearance shows that the ideas persisted. The records don’t establish that every service or data set did. CyberBiota’s first dated log gives us a new starting point with a build we can follow component by component.
entry.summary: Before CyberBiota, the lab was a collection of scripts. An inventory, a health check, and a ticket system gave those jobs a place to live.

entry.title: The failed checks stayed in the report

link.title: The failed checks stayed in the report

entry.content:
By October, CyberBiota3 was testing what local assistants could do with the evidence the lab collected. One exercise ran read-only diagnostics in parallel with normal operation. The aim was to see whether two roles could produce acceptable diagnostic results in scheduled windows. The roles were distinct, and their scores needed to stay separate for the comparison to mean anything.

Over a day with 96 scheduled windows per role, one role produced 96 accepted results. The other produced 87. That second result was about 91 percent against a 95 percent requirement. The gap mattered because it was measured against the intended run window, with the scheduled checks and failures all included.

The investigation led to a narrow change in how the diagnostics handled data. A later sample returned 16 accepted results out of 16 for the first role and 15 out of 15 for the second. That was useful evidence about the corrected setup in a shorter run. Replacing the original day with the shorter result would have left anyone reading the report unable to tell what had been tried before the correction.

The decision recorded both results. It accepted a limited read-only use and preserved the earlier reliability exception. Full incident handling, external delivery, and remediation were separate questions. The record doesn’t support judging all future runs from either sample.

I want the blog to keep that distinction whenever a repair improves a test. What failed, what was corrected, and what happened on the next run each get their own line in the story. A clean follow-up can explain why the work continued. It doesn’t need to erase the result that made the correction necessary.
entry.summary: A later clean sample helped isolate the problem. The original day still included failures, and the accepted scope stayed limited.

entry.title: The first CyberBiota build and the empty dashboard

link.title: The first CyberBiota build and the empty dashboard

entry.content:
The first dated CyberBiota build log opens on February 13. Proxmox is the host, ZFS is the storage layer, and an LXC guest runs Docker, Ansible, InfluxDB, and Grafana. The entries say that metrics arrived in InfluxDB. That confirmed one part of the route from the host to the dashboard. It would take until late that evening to see how narrow that success was.

At 10:40 p.m. the log marked dashboard recovery successful after changes to the collector and monitoring configuration. At 11:23, the data was still in InfluxDB and Grafana could connect to the data source, but the panels were empty. At 11:34, the work was paused. The log says InfluxDB saw no queries during a later check. Possible causes were still open, including how the data source or browser was making the request. The order matters. The earlier success entry describes the state of the investigation at that point. A reader looking for a working dashboard needed the later entries too.

The next day’s work followed more than one lead. The log describes using explicit organization and bucket IDs in the InfluxDB data source. It also describes Grafana failing to load a provisioned dashboard until the JSON was normalized. The two metric sources needed different queries as well. The Proxmox host metrics used a different CPU field and scale from the Telegraf inputs. A dashboard designed for one source could quietly misread or miss the other. Those corrections are recorded separately, so I don’t have to pick a single cause for every symptom that night.

What can I show from the records? The host produced metrics. A database received them. Grafana had trouble provisioning and querying the right data, and the following log records targeted corrections. The records I have leave the original rendered panels and exact component versions incomplete. An independent check of the whole deployment would have to reopen those questions.

The lasting value of that build is the separation between each test. Check that the host emitted the metric, that the database stored it, that the query names the right field and units, and that the panel actually shows the expected result. If the first three work and the fourth fails, the journal still has a useful answer about where to look next.
entry.summary: Proxmox was sending metrics to InfluxDB, yet Grafana showed empty panels. The next day’s corrections reveal where the checks fell short.

entry.title: Testing Dockhand before changing container management

link.title: Testing Dockhand before changing container management

entry.content:
The change on November 11 was an evaluation of Dockhand as a day-to-day container management interface. The practical question was whether it could replace the parts of Portainer used to investigate a service. The existing interface stayed in place during the evaluation, and the lab kept its Compose deployment files as the source for service configuration.

Check Recorded result What it supports
Compare container lists Dockhand and Docker reported the same 97 containers, including 72 running. Inventory matched at the time of the comparison.
Open a live log stream The report captured a working stream. An operator could watch a container’s logs during a check.
Compare resource readings Memory matched in the sample. CPU readings differed slightly between polls. The sampled readings were consistent enough for inspection.
Check application sign-in An unauthenticated inventory request returned HTTP 401 after native authentication was configured. That request was blocked without an application session.

The report also inspected the Docker socket’s bind mount. That check established the mount setting. The documented test did not demonstrate which Docker API operations the application could call. That authorization question matters before choosing a permanent management interface.

The report records the start of a planned observation period. It does not record the outcome of that period or a completed Portainer retirement.

Running the two tools in parallel made the change easier to assess. There was already a working interface available if the new one failed during the comparison. It also made the success criteria easier to state: the pilot demonstrated selected investigation tasks, while continued operation and any cutover required separate evidence.
entry.summary: A November change note on the Dockhand pilot, what its checks established, and why cutover is a separate decision.

entry.title: Why CyberBiota 2 moved to bare-metal Ubuntu

link.title: Why CyberBiota 2 moved to bare-metal Ubuntu

entry.content:
On April 6 the log records a fleet of Proxmox guests being moved onto a native software-defined network. The virtual gateway work had already taken several turns. The March records describe a failed OPNsense restoration and an unreliable VyOS installation attempt. A later summary describes the gateway differently. I can show the attempts and the April decision to leave those separate gateways behind. I can’t establish every intermediate working state from the records.

Access had already become part of the problem. The March 14 notes describe an SSH lockout after changes to the management network and access conditions. They also describe how little room there was to recover on a laptop being operated without a local console in normal use. Having a path from the proxy to the application would not solve that problem. The person operating the host still needed a way back in if a network change failed.

The last Proxmox evening shows the amount of work a network move could create. The log records changing guest network configuration, restarting the guests, and updating the reverse proxy’s backend targets. Uptime Kuma remained reachable during the recorded check, and the proxy was able to reach checked backends. That gave some confidence in the change. It did not establish that every application workflow was available to every client.

The next morning, April 7, the transition record calls for replacing that virtualization layout with a clean Ubuntu 25.10 installation. Docker would run on the host. A separate NVMe drive was set aside for persistent application data and model storage. The record reports that Ubuntu detected the GPU and that the driver check passed. The decision notes cite memory pressure, scheduling constraints, and the complexity of passing shell commands through several systems. Those are the recorded reasons for reducing the number of layers. I don’t have a before-and-after benchmark that quantifies their effect.

This was CyberBiota 2. It was a fresh installation with a different failure model. It moved more responsibility onto a single host for storage, permissions, and recovery. The records identify the new layout and the original Ubuntu release. They do not supply a verified migration list for every application and volume. Later records refer to Ubuntu 26.04. Whether that change was an upgrade or another reinstall is still open. I can say what the rebuild was designed to simplify and what its first checks showed, while keeping each of those unknowns attached to the transition.
entry.summary: A final Proxmox network migration was followed the next morning by a fresh Ubuntu install. That choice changed the lab’s network, storage, and hardware boundaries.

entry.title: The first backup I could show how to restore

link.title: The first backup I could show how to restore

entry.content:
The first recovery proof in CyberBiota3 had a narrow target: get the project repository back from an encrypted backup. That made the result possible to check. The repository contains the instructions and change records I would need in a rebuild. Live application data needed a different test with its own backup and consistency requirements.

The June work initialized a local Restic backup repository and recorded the exclusions before the run. Those exclusions were part of the proof. The backup was meant to include the selected project files without bringing in known sensitive configuration or runtime paths. After the backup, the record confirmed a snapshot existed. The work then restored it into a separate test folder. It could be inspected without putting recovered files over the working copy.

The validation names examples that came back: the README, the operations instructions, and the backup plan. The report also records checking the restored tree for excluded paths. That is more informative than a screenshot saying the backup ran. It gives a reader something to look for in the result and explains why the destination was separate. The records I relied on do not establish an independently verified count of everything restored, so I’ve left that number out.

The July 6 timer receipt adds another test. It records a later scheduled backup running without someone starting it by hand. That’s useful evidence about unattended execution on that occasion. The June restore showed that selected files could be recovered. The July timer showed a scheduled run could take place. Each result is worth keeping because either side can fail independently.

The boundary is clear enough to carry forward. This was a local repository recovery exercise. I can’t use it to promise recovery of a live database, a replacement host, or a copy stored off site. Those are follow-on drills. The June proof matters because a future drill has something concrete to improve on: pick a recovery target, restore it in isolation, and verify what came back and what stayed out.
entry.summary: A local encrypted snapshot, a restore into a test directory, and a later timer receipt answered different parts of the recovery question.

entry.title: The rise of CyberBiota3
entry.content:
It was time for a fresh start in my home lab. I had already built AriseOne, and I would try two versions of CyberBiota before reaching the one I wanted to keep building. Those earlier versions taught me different things. CyberBiota3 is where I brought those lessons together.

AriseOne had started with small jobs: a health script, a list of hosts for Ansible, and a way to keep track of updates. By early February it had a Proxmox host, a file service, a dashboard, and a ticket system. The lab already had real work to do. I wanted a fresh start, and the next records show what that first CyberBiota looked like: Proxmox again, with ZFS for storage and an LXC guest bringing Docker, Ansible, and monitoring together. The records preserve both setups. They leave open exactly which AriseOne files and application data made it across.

The first CyberBiota stretched the virtualized design. The log followed a metric from Proxmox into InfluxDB and still ended the night with empty Grafana panels. Network changes added their own dependencies. After experiments with virtual gateways, I moved the lab to Ubuntu on April 7, with Docker running on the host. That became CyberBiota 2. The earlier record names Ubuntu 25.10. May records refer to 26.04, but they do not show whether I upgraded in place or rebuilt again.

By June, the CyberBiota3 records looked different. They kept the initial failure alongside the retry, separated a working route from a working application, and treated a restore as its own test. I still changed my mind about tools. I had removed n8n in April, then reconsidered it after reading about a practical homelab use for it. By June I was running it again. I also rolled back a webhook pilot that delivered its event under settings I couldn’t keep.

That is the home lab this blog follows. I want you to see what I changed, why I kept or reversed it, and how far I got before the next problem began. The chapters below follow that thread from the January scripts to the tests and operating decisions that define CyberBiota3 for me.
entry.summary: I wanted a fresh start for my home lab. CyberBiota3 brought together what I had learned building AriseOne and the first two versions of CyberBiota.

entry.title: A valid Compose file and a failed deployment

link.title: A valid Compose file and a failed deployment

entry.content:
The June 26 Compose check passed. Then Docker couldn’t pull two declared images, and the first deployment stopped. The file was shaped correctly enough to parse. The registry couldn’t supply the tags it named. Those checks were testing different things, and the first report leaves the pull failure in place as the outcome of the first attempt.

For the retry, the replacement image tags were checked against registry manifests. That removed the first blocker. Infisical then restarted repeatedly. Its encryption and authentication inputs were present in the deployment, but didn’t match the format and length the app expected. Correcting those inputs called for a targeted recreation of Infisical. Its Postgres and Redis containers were left in place.

Homarr failed on a separate path. Its route returned HTTP 500, and its service definition wasn’t passing a required encryption key into the container. The repair added that mapping and recreated just Homarr. The next route check returned HTTP 307 and went to the first-run setup screen. A reader can see the difference immediately: the old server error was gone and the setup route answered. There is no test of a completed setup in that result.

The remaining route checks tell a similar story at a wider level. Four selected routes responded with HTTP 200. The test proves those responses for the named check window. The next level of assurance would be an actual application job, such as signing in and doing a normal operation. The retry result shows the last completed step with enough detail for the next person to decide what to test.

The way I would read a deployment now is in that order. Can the configuration be rendered? Can the artifacts actually be fetched? Does the application initialize with the supplied inputs? Can a person finish the job they came to do? Those questions also put a limit on the repair. The broken image names did not justify recreating a database, and the missing Homarr input did not tell me anything about how Infisical had been configured. Leaving the healthy dependencies alone made the retry easier to interpret.
entry.summary: The first CyberBiota3 deployment failed before images could pull. On the retry, two applications needed different repairs.

entry.title: The webhook worked. I still rolled it back.

link.title: The webhook worked. I still rolled it back.

entry.content:
The point of the pilot was straightforward. A change in a Git-backed service should reach an n8n workflow without a person carrying the event between the two. The test delivered an event. For a few minutes, the integration did what it was built to do.

The problem was in the conditions of the test. The pilot made outbound destinations more permissive and relaxed certificate verification. It proved delivery under those conditions. The lab needed an integration that could prove delivery with the intended destination and transport protections in place. Keeping the working pilot would have carried those temporary conditions into normal operation.

The June 30 rollback record gives an exact scope. The pilot webhook was deleted from the source service, and its associated workflow was removed from n8n. The temporary transport settings were reverted. The underlying applications remained available for other work. It was the integration that had failed acceptance, even though the delivery trial had succeeded.

There are at least two distinct checks in a test like this. One asks whether the intended receiver got the event and did something with it. The other asks whether the sender could reach only the intended receiver and verify the connection. A successful response can answer the delivery question without answering the trust question. The pilot record and rollback are how I can tell those two results apart now.

Later work can use this baseline without treating it as a finished replacement. Return to a narrow destination and verified connection, then repeat the delivery check. If either check fails, keep the attempt documented in its actual state. That preserves why the original test was useful and why leaving it in place would have been the wrong next step.
entry.summary: The event arrived, but the pilot had changed the transport protections. The rollback removed the integration and kept the applications.

entry.title: Why I removed n8n and brought it back

link.title: Why I removed n8n and brought it back

entry.content:
n8n was removed on April 8, the day after the move to native Ubuntu. The operations log gives a reason: the new build was trying agent-driven automation in place of older workflows. The same part of the log records work on an assistant gateway and a connection to a local model. The log establishes what the rebuild was trying to do. It doesn’t tell me that every older workflow was replaced or where the original workflow data ended up.

At the time I didn’t see much use for n8n. I reconsidered after reading a Virtualization Howto article about using workflow automation and AI in a home lab. The example made it worth looking at the tool again. I don’t have a record of the exact feature I had in mind or the date I read it, so those details aren’t part of the claim. The change in my view is something I remember. Its return is also visible in the June deployment records.

The June 26 record shows n8n deployed as part of CyberBiota3. Later route checks returned HTTP 200 for the selected n8n path. That established reachability on that run. It didn’t establish that a particular workflow would receive an event, execute the right steps, or handle a failure the way I wanted.

The June 30 webhook pilot gave a more concrete test. A source service produced an event and the automation received it. The pilot had loosened transport settings to make that happen, so it was rolled back. The webhook and its workflow were removed. The underlying applications, including n8n, remained in the lab. That sequence can be hard to follow in an undated inventory. It makes sense when the removal, return, and rollback are treated as three separate events.

Bringing the tool back gave me room to test bounded workflows on their own terms. The record still leaves the earlier data disposition open. It proves the later installation and a narrow pilot, with the pilot’s reversal right beside it. That’s a more useful description of how I use tools in this lab than a list that simply marks n8n installed.
entry.summary: The April build moved toward agent-driven work. A practical home lab article made me reconsider what a visible workflow engine was good for.
